spec.title: Evidence from the responsible subsystems
spec.intro:
You are handed one Windows endpoint — WIN-LAB04 — and asked to produce a single
machine-readable evidence bundle an auditor can read against SOC 2 CC6: disk
encryption, endpoint-protection posture, the effective screen-lock setting, recent
failed sign-ins, and who holds local administrator rights. Then make the whole thing
re-runnable, so the same machine can be re-evidenced next quarter and compared.
This console is a simulated Windows PowerShell 5.1 session. No real PowerShell engine
exists for the browser, so every output here is produced by an object pipeline that
follows PowerShell's documented formatting rules and this module's own committed lab
fixtures — and where the simulation has a boundary, it says so in plain text instead
of pretending to be Windows.

tasks.instruction:
Ask the subsystem that owns the encryption claim. Run `Get-BitLockerVolume` bare
and look at what comes back — an object with named properties, not a paragraph.
Then ask precisely: `Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: | Select-Object MountPoint,
VolumeStatus`. Write down, in words, which subsystem owns the claim and which
property decides it.

hints.nudge: On Windows you never go looking for a file — you ask the responsible subsystem. BitLocker owns this claim; `Select-Object` keeps only the properties the control cares about.

hints.concept: §4.2 — BitLocker owns the encryption claim; `VolumeStatus` decides it

hints.reveal: Get-BitLockerVolume, then: Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C: | Select-Object MountPoint, VolumeStatus

tasks.explain:
`VolumeStatus = FullyEncrypted` is the pass condition, and it arrived as a typed
property — you selected it by name, you didn't parse text. This is the same
laptop-encryption claim this curriculum keeps re-asking; here the operating
system's own subsystem answered it directly.

tasks.instruction:
One query, the whole endpoint-protection posture: run `Get-MpComputerStatus |
Select-Object AntivirusEnabled, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, AntivirusSignatureAge`.
Note which property proves "enabled" and which proves "current" — installed,
enabled, and current are three different facts.

hints.nudge: Defender hands back ONE status object carrying the whole posture. Pick the three properties that prove the words 'on' and 'up to date' — presence proves neither.

hints.concept: §4.3 — installed is not enabled, and enabled is not current

tasks.explain:
A control that only checked installation would pass a machine whose protection was
switched off in January. You evidenced the behavioral properties — enabled and
current — which is what makes this reading mean something to an auditor.

tasks.instruction:
Read the EFFECTIVE screen-lock timeout straight from the registry:
`(Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Control Panel\Desktop' -Name ScreenSaveTimeOut).ScreenSaveTimeOut`.
Then ask the policy engine what was INTENDED — run `gpresult` bare first and read
its complaint, then run `gpresult /R`. One of those two results is a collection
error and one is evidence; note the difference, and why your bundle must cite the
effective value rather than the intended one.

hints.nudge: The registry holds what the machine is actually doing; the policy tool reports what it was told to do. gpresult refuses to run without a scope — its error text tells you which switch the report needs.

hints.concept: §4.4 — what was intended (policy) is not always what is effective (the registry value in force)

tasks.explain:
`ERROR: Invalid syntax.` was a collection error — your question was malformed; the
machine was never non-compliant. That distinction is rubric material. The registry
said 600 seconds is in force (effective); the RSoP report shows the screen-lock
policy that was applied (intended). Defensible evidence cites what the endpoint is
actually doing.

tasks.instruction:
Pull the recent failed sign-ins from the Security event log: `Get-WinEvent
-FilterHashtable @{ LogName='Security'; Id=4625 } -MaxEvents 20 | Select-Object
TimeCreated, Id`. Then count them mechanically with
`(Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625} -MaxEvents 20).Count`.

hints.nudge: Failed sign-ins are structured records under one well-known event ID. The filter is a hashtable — log name plus ID — and `.Count` on the parenthesized query counts what came back.

hints.concept: §4.5 — the log is structured data you query; records arrive as objects, so you filter by Id and read TimeCreated

hints.reveal: Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName='Security'; Id=4625 } -MaxEvents 20 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, then: (Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625} -MaxEvents 20).Count

tasks.explain:
Three failures in thirteen seconds reads very differently from three across three
days — and because the records are typed objects, your collector simply records
the count. Whether 3 crosses a threshold is the EVALUATE stage's judgment, not the
collector's.

tasks.instruction:
Read the standing-privilege claim from the local account database: run
`Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators`, then select just the names with
`(Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators).Name`. Note why faithfully recording
this membership is LOCATE/QUERY work, and why deciding "is this membership
correct?" belongs to a different loop stage.

hints.nudge: The local account database owns this claim. The bare command shows the member objects; member access on the parenthesized query keeps just the property the bundle needs.

hints.concept: §4.6 — the endpoint can only tell you who is in the group; judging the membership against an approved list is EVALUATE

tasks.explain:
The endpoint told you who holds local-admin rights — that is everything it CAN
tell you. Whether that membership is correct requires an approved list the machine
doesn't have, which is exactly why collection and evaluation are different loop
stages with different owners.

tasks.instruction:
Assemble the readings into one `[pscustomobject]` whose field names map to SOC 2
CC6 controls, and export it two ways: pipe it to `ConvertTo-Json > bundle.json`,
then build the same object again and pipe it to `Export-Csv bundle.csv
-NoTypeInformation`. Read both files back with `Get-Content` to confirm they hold
your readings — and look closely at the CSV's LocalAdmins cell.

hints.nudge: Each hashtable entry is ControlLabel = (Get-Subsystem).Property — the five readings you already made, wrapped in [pscustomobject]@{ } and piped to an exporter. The evidence must be PRODUCED by the pipeline, not typed in by hand.

hints.concept: §5.4 — shaping selected properties into a labeled, control-mapped record

hints.reveal: [pscustomobject]@{ Control_CC6_1_Encryption = (Get-BitLockerVolume -MountPoint C:).VolumeStatus; Control_CC6_8_DefenderEnabled = (Get-MpComputerStatus).AntivirusEnabled; Control_CC6_1_ScreenLockTimeoutSeconds = (Get-ItemProperty 'HKCU:\Control Panel\Desktop' -Name ScreenSaveTimeOut).ScreenSaveTimeOut; Control_CC6_1_FailedLogonCount = (Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4625} -MaxEvents 20).Count; Control_CC6_3_LocalAdmins = (Get-LocalGroupMember -Group Administrators).Name } | ConvertTo-Json > bundle.json — then the same object | Export-Csv bundle.csv -NoTypeInformation, then Get-Content bundle.json and Get-Content bundle.csv

tasks.explain:
Every field is named for the control it evidences, and every value came from a
`Get-` query — the bundle is a record an auditor can read without knowing
PowerShell. The CSV's `System.Object[]` cell is real Export-Csv behavior: a CSV
cell is flat text, so the admin LIST survived only in the JSON. That wrinkle is
why the bundle ships in both shapes.

tasks.instruction:
Make it re-runnable: open the editor with `notepad Collect-EndpointCompliance.ps1`
and put your sequence in it — a comment naming what it is, your two export
pipelines from t6, and a final `Get-Content bundle.json` so each run prints the
bundle it produced. Every command must be a read-only `Get-` (a collector that
mutates is an intervention, not evidence). Save, exit, and run
`.\Collect-EndpointCompliance.ps1` twice. The checker will also re-run your script
in two clean, clock-perturbed sessions and compare the evidence. Then write down
one control this endpoint script structurally cannot prove, and which cloud
subsystem owns it.

hints.nudge: A script is just the lines you already ran, saved. The editor opens with `notepad <file>`; the read-only rule means every command in it starts with Get- (gpresult and the exporters read and write files, they don't change the endpoint).

hints.concept: §4.8 — read-only by construction: a collector observes and changes nothing, which is what makes its output trustworthy as evidence

hints.reveal: notepad Collect-EndpointCompliance.ps1 — paste a # comment, your t6 ConvertTo-Json > bundle.json pipeline, your t6 Export-Csv bundle.csv -NoTypeInformation pipeline, and Get-Content bundle.json — save with Ctrl+O, exit with Ctrl+X, then run .\Collect-EndpointCompliance.ps1 twice

tasks.explain:
Identical evidence twice, from clean sessions with different clocks — that is the
difference between "we verified this once" and "we can re-evidence this machine
next quarter and diff the bundles." And the bundle stays honest about its
boundary: MFA enforcement, sign-in location blocking, device-compliance gating —
those decisions happen in Entra ID conditional access at sign-in time, and their
evidence lives in the cloud's logs (Module 06 reaches it by API). An endpoint
script that claimed to prove them would be lying.

tasks.instruction:
In 5–7 sentences, as if to a colleague who has never opened PowerShell: which
subsystem owns each of the five control claims; why you selected properties
instead of parsing text (objects, not text streams); why effective beats intended
for the screen-lock; what the failed-logon count does and does not prove; why the
collector is built entirely from `Get-`; and the one control that belongs to
Entra ID, not the endpoint.

hints.nudge: The §3 mental model: a claim is owned by a named subsystem; you ask it with a Get- command; the answer is an object whose properties you select; and some claims' truth never touches the endpoint at all.

hints.concept: §3 — The Mental Model; §4.7 — drawing the AD/Entra ID seam honestly

_notes: Module 04 simulated endpoint WIN-LAB04 (compliant posture) — typed object stores per
subsystem, per module 04 prose (§3-§5) and the committed lab fixture
BitLocker C: FullyEncrypted 100; Defender enabled, signature age 1; screen-lock 600s;
exactly three Security-log 4625 events at 5/27/2026 9:13:50/9:13:58/9:14:03 PM;
ScreenSaveTimeOut is seeded NUMERIC per the module's canonical bundle (real REG_SZ is a
string '600' — documented divergence, DESIGN-INPUTS fidelity note 6).
Defender property set beyond the module's three taught properties carries names from the
Microsoft Learn Get-MpComputerStatus reference (representative values), so the bare cmdlet
honestly renders as a >4-property list. Event Message strings are the documented event
summaries (4624/4625/4672). gpresultReportFile resolves to the authored RSoP fixture;
loaders strip its single trailing newline when seeding gpresultReport.
